message.content:
In Texas, tenants have several statutory protections and responsibilities under the Texas Property Code and related laws. Here’s an overview of your key rights: | Category | What You’re Entitled To | |----------|------------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlords may charge up to one month’s rent (or two if the lease is for a furnished unit).
• Must return the deposit within 30 days after you move out, minus any lawful deductions. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must keep the premises safe, sanitary, and in good repair.
• Must maintain plumbing, heating, electrical, and structural integrity. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • Landlord cannot enter without notice (except emergencies) or disturb your peaceful use. | | **Notice Requirements** | • For non‑payment of rent: 3‑day written notice before eviction.
• For lease termination: 30‑day notice for month‑to‑month agreements; 60‑days for longer leases. | | **Eviction Process** | • Must follow court procedures; no “self‑help” evictions (e.g., changing locks). | | **Discrimination Protections** | • Landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income. | | **Repair & Deduct / Rent Withhold** | • If landlord fails to fix major problems, you may repair and deduct from rent or withhold rent until repairs are made (subject to limits). | | **Lease Terms** | • Lease must be in writing if it lasts longer than one year.
• Certain clauses (e.g., “no pets”) can be challenged if they violate fair housing laws. | | **Rent Control** | • Texas has no statewide rent‑control law; however, local ordinances may apply in some cities. | | **Utilities** | • Landlord must provide water, electricity, gas, and heat unless otherwise specified. | | **Insurance** | • Tenants are not required to carry renters’ insurance, but it’s highly recommended. | ### How to Protect Your Rights 1. **Document Everything** – Keep copies of all communications, receipts, and photos of any damage or maintenance issues. 2. **Know the Law** – Familiarize yourself with the Texas Property Code sections relevant to your situation (e.g., §§ 92.001–92.021 for security deposits). 3. **Use Written Notices** – Send notices via certified mail or email with read receipts to establish proof. 4. **Seek Legal Aid** – If disputes arise, consult a local attorney or tenant advocacy group. If you need more detailed guidance—such as drafting a lease or a notice of intent to vacate—just let me know!
